Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

vignette: John, a 39-year-old divorced man of Oceania descent and an airline pilot by profession, has been struggling with intense distress since a traumatic incident involving law enforcement. The event left him feeling profoundly shaken and has significantly impacted his daily life. The trauma occurred during a routine flight from Sydney to Brisbane. Mid-flight, he noticed unusual activity in the cockpit; someone had tampered with critical equipment. Before he could react, armed police burst into the cabin, identifying themselves as part of an anti-terror unit. They apprehended him and another crew member for questioning. The entire ordeal was surreal and terrifying, leaving John haunted by memories that feel more real than any other experiences in his life. John describes his memories of this event as vivid and almost too real, which often brings back the same overwhelming terror he felt during the incident. This intense recall has led to several triggers that have become deeply ingrained in his daily routine. For instance, simply feeling nauseous can bring the memory back with a visceral punch, making him feel like he’s reliving the trauma. His job as an airline pilot, while typically structured and reliable, now holds new dangers for John. The mere act of driving to work with colleagues or being in close proximity to others triggers anxiety that something bad is about to happen. This heightened sense of threat often starts when delays occur—any unexpected holdup makes him jump to the worst-case scenario. Ordinary sounds that most people wouldn’t notice startle him, and he feels constantly vigilant, always on edge. John’s fear of strangers approaching has worsened over time. In his line of work, meeting new people is inevitable, but now even a casual interaction can set off a wave of anxiety. He believes that any stranger could be a threat, and this belief only intensifies the terror he feels when remembering the traumatic event. The memories feel so vivid that they reinforce his sense of danger in everyday situations. John's work environment has also been affected. His colleagues have noticed that he avoids driving with others and is often distracted during flights, which can lead to a sense of unease among his crew members. These avoidance behaviors are not just a matter of personal discomfort; they create real tension at work, where trust and cooperation are crucial. The more John feels threatened by ordinary situations, the more vivid and terrifying his memories become. This cycle has made it increasingly difficult for him to function normally. He is now on edge in almost every situation, constantly anticipating something bad happening. The cumulative effect of this heightened threat monitoring and trigger sensitivity has taken a toll on his mental health. What finally brought John to seek help was the realization that he could no longer manage these overwhelming feelings without professional assistance. His fear is most acute when he thinks about continuing in his career as an airline pilot, where unexpected delays or interactions with strangers are inevitable. Yet, he hopes for a way to regain control and peace of mind, enabling him to return to work without the constant fear that has become a part of his daily life. John's narrative reveals a deeply interwoven loop of triggers leading to heightened threat perceptions, which in turn intensify his memories and reinforce his sense of danger. This self-reinforcing cycle has made it increasingly difficult for him to navigate both his personal and professional life without significant distress.
